1. Summary of the Article

This systematic overview by Abashidze-Gabaidze et al. explores the place of primary health care (PHC) as an anchor for an unhealthy-free society, both locally and globally. The writers address the opportunities and threats confronting strengthened PHC system building, focusing on implications for policymakers and practical advice. The study reviews the synthesis of evidence from several sources that indicate PHC's relevance to achieving equitable health gains and sustainable development. The study is relevant specifically to Georgia and the region of the Caucasus, whereby PHC system building has clear opportunities and threats due to limited resources, as well as historical context.

2. Strengths of the Article

Strengths Relevance and Timeliness: The paper touches on an incredibly relevant, time-specific topic whereby primary health care have risen as an invaluable building brick of health systems globally. The focus on Georgia, as well as the region of the Caucasus, adds immense worth, considering the clear opportunities confronting this region.

Comprehensive Methodology: Mixed-methods approach, narrative synthesis, complemented by documents' analysis, best suited to analyze complexities of PHC. Including recent (2002–2023) studies add credibility. A vast overview over many years confirms that primary health care does not disappear. However, it has not emerged - the gold standard, strengthening it - so this extensive-scale overview makes scope, analysis, and comparison possible for recommendations. In this, the authors have - a Prisma diagram of study selection, PRISMA Checklist, added, additionally, Table N1, showing the level, expertise, responsibility, diligence while preparing the paper, focusing, as per importance, need, importance, by evaluating, strengthening, prioritizing, first, primary health care by nations, including Georgia, also by greater well-being, by reviewing, analyzing, studying 38 papers over primary health care, prepared over many years, over many nations, additionally, confirming importance, relevance, of the paper, that strengthening, enhancing, primary health care must remain an agenda both over Georgia, also over general system, over healthcare, over the whole world.

Practical Recommendations: The paper makes implementable, practical recommendations, recommendations especially by policymaking authorities, especially over low- and middle-income nations (LMICs) like Georgia. These areas, especially staffing, funding, and infrastructure, are beneficial.

Global, Local Context: The overview balances well both global priorities (for example, the importance accorded by WHO over universal health coverage) and local issues, so it serves well both international and local stakeholders.

3. Weaknesses, Areas Improvable

Important Points:

Limited Access to Information: Authors are aware of the problem posed by the inability to attain access to detailed, accurate information, especially in Georgia. Although this must have been due to the region's limitations, it would have benefited if there had been an increased description of how these limitations affected findings and recommendations.

Limitations of Narrative Synthesis:Although narrative synthesis fits this type of overview, lack of meta-analysis may not always make it possible to offer sound statistical findings. However, this is only minor due to the qualitative study.

Minor Points:

Specific Detailing Recommendations:Recommendations concerning implementation strategies, especially by Georgia, are vague. An example includes how proposed policies must be localized by considering the limitations of the local environment.

4. Relevance and Contribution

Contribution to Literature

The paper contributes well to the burgeoning corpus of work relating to primary health care, especially in Georgia and the region of the Caucasus. Findings are relevant to policymaking and researchers and practitioners are intent on developing strengthened health systems. Practical recommendations add substance to the paper, especially if they have implications for areas similarly challenged.

5. Final Recommendation

This is an exhaustively conducted systematized review of an absolutely fundamental topic. Despite limitations due to data unavailability, coupled with the adversities experienced by Georgia, the authors have conducted an exhaustive, perceptive analysis. Minor flaws are not enough to blemish the quality and worthiness of the paper. Hence, this paper is very strongly recommended for indexing. It shall be an excellent addition to the field and an invaluable tool, and it shall remain so for scholars, policymakers, and practitioners involved in strengthening PHC across the region. Apart from minor criticisms, this work shall be handy and one of the best across the region, especially in Georgia. Papers like this must get indexed so that they act as an encouragement factor to make other scholars think beyond the scope of this paper while widening the scope of their work.

Further Comments

Acknowledging Limitations: Appreciation must be accorded here; it must be noted that the adversities experienced by the authors while carrying out this review, especially owing to data unavailability coupled with insufficiency across Georgia, must be appreciated. These limitations are endemic across LMICs, and does this deem down the relevance across findings? Instead, these underscore the need for increased international support, especially coordination, to strengthen the PHC system across these nations.

Value across Georgia: The paper is especially valuable across Georgia, as it has an agenda of bridging PHC service deficits. The recommendations are practical, localised, and, thus, very actionable across policymaking circles and the healthcare service delivery system.

Conclusion

This systematic analysis adds significantly to the literature review on strengthening PHC, particularly for Georgia and the Caucasus region. Given writers' challenges, this study has practical implications and sound contributions toward strengthening the PHC system. The paper has minor flaws that outweigh these, which warrants my highest recommendation.

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard.

The revisions to the paper have helped clarify what the authors did or did not do and brought to light the need for further revisions. The authors have undertaken a lot of work, but the additional revisions required are entirely manageable.

My principle points are:

1. This is not a systematic review, but could reasonably be described as a selective review. The literature search, the inclusion and exclusion of articles, and the narrative synthesis all indicate a selective rather than systematic approach. If, as stated in the introduction, the overall aim is to provide guidance to the development of primary health care in Georgia, a selective review is reasonable. It enables the authors to select evidence and messages tailored to the prevailing situation in Georgia.

2. The article needs a careful edit. There is quite a bit of duplication and various grammatical errors that could be usefully corrected. Could the Journal editors help the authors with this?

Further detailed points are included below.

Introduction

A reference is needed for the statement that 80% of global deaths are attributable to chronic conditions.

A reference is also needed to support the statement that 90% of UHC interventions can be implemented through primary health care (PHC). Both these statements may be over-stating the case.

The outline of the problems of PHC in Georgia is a welcome addition and leads in to the aim of the paper – to develop recommendations to improve PHC in Georgia. Some words are missing from the subsequent paragraph, highlighted with square brackets.

The introduction offers a broad overview of PHC. Mention of WHO’s definition and view of PHC is relevant, but there is a lot of duplication in the following paragraphs that could usefully be omitted.

Methods

The search strategy is described and appears extensive. The inclusion of a copy of the strategy for each bibliographic database is unnecessary, but it would be wise to include in a supplementary at least on search strategy as an example, ideally PubMed. The PRISMA chart indicates that 57 articles were identified from the database searching. This is a very low number if it refers to the articles listed in the databases – the number of hits relating to primary health care would be expected to be many thousands. Some explanation of the small number of articles included is needed. The inclusion and exclusion criteria were quite broad and it’s possible that they allowed room for subjective judgments about an article’s eligibility for inclusion. The selection of articles, according to the inclusion/exclusion criteria, were influenced by whether they were regarded as ‘pertinent’, an approach that should not be regarded as systematic.

The Table of included studies is helpful. It describes each of the studies clearly, although only 27 articles were in the Table but 38 were included in the review. They are a heterogenous group of articles, both in terms of design and topic. Some of the articles are discussion or opinion pieces; for example, reference 34 is a commentary and reference 9 is a book that describes the US health care system. This means that the review is not systematic. I’m not clear how risk of bias tools would have been applied to these discussion pieces. A narrative synthesis was undertaken, a suitable approach given the nature of the papers that were included.

The Results section draws out many of the weaknesses in the delivery of PHC in various countries. Some information on the included articles is presented at the end of the results section but a summary of the numbers of hits and articles included should be at the start of the results section.

A Conclusions section provides further evidence, and a set of 13 recommendations is then presented. The conclusions section could be re-drafted to concentrate on what needs to be done next to strengthen PHC rather than summarize findings from a few of the included papers. The recommendations may well be directed at the health system in Georgia although this is not stated explicitly. If this is intended, it should be made clear. Ending the paper on messages for the Georgia health system would tie in well with the remarks in the introduction.

The authors do not report when the search was conducted, but state that the search was limited to last 10 years. They have however, cherry picked articles published 2002-2008, and then included studies spanning 2010-2023. This inconsistency is highly irregular and would not be considered appropriate for a systematic review.

I'm not a topic expert, so this paper may well be considered to be a well argued narrative literature review. From a methodological point of view, the search methods are not sufficiently reported for it to be considered a systematic review.

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to state that I do not consider it to be of an acceptable scientific standard, for reasons outlined above.

Overview

Congratulations to the authors for making the case that primary health care is key to the effectiveness of health systems. Round the world, primary health care needs strengthening both to improve population health and to increase the efficiency of health services.

Although others have reviewed the effects of primary health care, this new study investigates gaps in care, in the lack of staff, shortages of funding, poor access to medicines, inadequate facilities and infrastructure, and inadequate training. The identification of these problems, shared by many countries, is important, and this constitutes a powerful message for policymakers – if they aim to improve the health of the people they are responsible for, they must strengthen primary health care.

Specific comments

The paper might be adjusted in a few ways to make it more accessible.

1. The Introduction covers a lot of relevant issues. Would it be worth saying something about primary health care in Georgia, if one aim of the paper is to inform the health system in George? Also, it is not clear why public health is given a paragraph on page 3. How does this fit in to the case for primary health care?

2. It would be better to use the term systematic review rather than meta-analysis. Meta-analysis implies a quantitative or statistical approach to combining the findings; the paper is does not involve a statistical analysis and is really a systematic review. A narrative synthesis (page 6) is not a meta-analysis.

3. The methods are generally well described and they indicate a careful approach was taken. It would be helpful to present more on the search strategy – would it be possible to include an example of the search strategy in a supplementary file?

4. A PRISMA chart would be helpful, and could be included in the supplementary materials (https://www.bmj.com/content/372/bmj.n71). This would help readers understand at what stage and why papers were excluded from the review. A very wide range of outcomes was included, and this could have led to a vast quantity of papers – how were they reduced down to the number in the review?

5. Care appears to have been taken in assessing the risk of bias in included studies. A standard format was used, for example.

6. The Results section needs to be re-ordered to first present basic information on the studies identified and the characteristics of those included. This information could be presented in a series of Tables that should show the country of origin, the outcomes of interest, and the findings of the assessment of risk of bias. Once this information has been reported, the findings can then be described. The findings themselves are interesting; the addition of tables describing the findings of each paper should help to explain the basis for the broad statements of the Results section.

7. The discussion section mentions the strengths and limitations of the study, and sets out a series of conclusions. There is some repetition across the discussion/ conclusions/ recommendations, and some editing would help. The conclusions and recommendations themselves are all reasonable.

8. The discussion might include a paragraph on how the review’s findings reflect those of other recent reviews of primary health care. This would help to show support the findings.

I hope the authors continue to conduct studies in this field. They have wishes for good luck in such an undertaking.

Editorial Note from the F1000Research Editorial Team: This peer-review report was originally published on 17th June 2024, and on 1st July 2024 the report was edited to include an additional paragraph provided by the reviewer relating to Reviewer 1's (Ruben Avendano-Herrera's) report for this article.

Review for: Isolation and complete genome sequence of 
                    Aeromonas bacteriophage Gekk3-15

This work details the method of isolation and sequencing of a novel bacteriophage that infects 
                Aeromonas veronii, as well as translations of the genome. This is a useful finding as the isolated phage shares a low degree of similarity to previously sequenced phages, and the most closely related phage infects a host belonging to a different genus.

Major comments: 
                The framing of the study may be too broad for the content. The abstract discusses the use of phage in 
                            Aeromonas 
                            hydrophila,but this is not tested in the main text, and it is unclear if this particular phage would infect this host. We recommend either re-framing the abstract to specify 
                            Aeromonas veronii only, as this is the only isolate tested, or to test the phage infectivity on 
                            A. hydrophilaalso. This is especially important if the aim of the phage isolation is to be used in phage therapy.

                -1' not '0,01 mg ml
                -1'

Please use 'L' rather than 'l' for litres as this removes possible confusion between 'l', 'I', and 1.'L' is the approved symbol for litre (
                https://www.nist.gov/pml/owm/si-units-volume).

The authors attempt to classify their phage into an appropriate taxonomy based on amino acid identity of structural proteins. While this is not the gold standard as recommended by the ICTV (nucleotide similarity across the genome as specified by VIRIDIC), it is probably as close as is possible, given the paucity of suitably similar reference genomes. For instance we attempted to identify the closest phage genome in both INPHARED (Cook et al., 2021
                1) and PhageClouds (Rangel-Pineros 
                et al., 2021
                2) (at both 0.15 and 0.2 distance), which yielded no hits. Therefore, the cautious interpretation of the placement by the authors is appropriate and should be revisited when more closely related genomes are deposited.

The reviewer Ruben Avendano-Herrera is incorrect in requesting that the authors use the term Myoviridae. This term was abandoned by the ICTV in their latest guidance which now requires the use of 'myovirus' to describe morphology, due to a lack of evidence for a shared common ancestor (Turner

Summary:

The full name of the species should be provided on its first mention: 
                Candida albicans. For subsequent references, use 
                C. albicans. Always use the correct spelling for species names according to taxonomy and binomial nomenclature; for example, it should be 
                Thymus vulgaris. The term Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry must be used instead of gas chromatography-mass spectrometer. Additionally, the conclusion should directly correspond to the research objective.

Introduction:

The authors could enhance the introduction by including more information about the potential applications of 
                T. vulgarisbased on other studies, particularly how it has been utilized in formulating experimental products for dentistry. References to consider include:

1.  Marinković J., et. al. (2022) -Ref 1

2.  Diouchi J., et. al. (2024)-Ref 2

3.  Marinković J., et. al. (2020) -Ref 3

It is important to correct the spelling throughout the text: it should be 
                Thymus vulgaris (
                T. vulgaris), not Thymus vularis.

Methods:

It is crucial to specify the calculation method for essential oil extraction yield. The authors mention that BHIB was used as the sample transport medium. However, the appropriate transport medium for isolating 
                C. albicans is Sabouraud. In terms of identification of 
                C. albicans, why wasn’t a specific identification method utilized? The authors should clarify whether methods such as CHROMagar, a urease test, or a cycloheximide resistance test were employed, as these are commonly used for species identification in laboratories.

In the GC-MS section, the term "Thyme vulgaris" is incorrect; "Thyme" refers to the common name in English and should not replace binomial nomenclature. It is also important to specify the library used for comparing the compounds during identification. In the sensitivity test, the authors did not indicate how repetitions were calculated for each concentration or the parameters used for this calculation. In the MIC and MBC section, the wording needs to be corrected to reflect "µL of each concentration in the ten wells."

In the statistical analysis section, it is essential to clarify that the one-way ANOVA test requires compliance with three main assumptions: independence of observations, normal distribution of the residuals, and homogeneity of the residuals. Concluding these last two assumptions based on the data alone can lead to misinterpretation. Authors should verify these assumptions to confirm the suitability of the ANOVA test and should indicate which multiple comparisons test was utilized.

Results:

From a methodological standpoint, it would have been ideal to first test the antifungal capacity of the essential oil and then prepare an experimental paste based on this concentration for comparison with the TAP.

Table 2 does not specify the statistical test used. It is misleading to mention Levene's test at the bottom of the table, as this only indicates homogeneity of variances. In fact, this table could also be used to present multiple comparisons using superscript letters, simplifying the presentation and avoiding the confusion caused by a lengthy Table 3.

Figure 1 unnecessarily reiterates information presented in the table.

Figure 2 displays Petri dishes with agar diffusion assays (wells) showing inhibition zones. However, the inhibition zones overlap, particularly evident in plate A between T and A. This overlap arises because the radial diffusion of the antimicrobials is too close together, making it impossible to delineate exact areas of inhibition for each agent. As a result, the zones become difficult to measure according to standard protocols, lacking a defined boundary between one inhibitor and another. According to CLSI (Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute, M100) and EUCAST (European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing), inhibition zones should: - Be measured in millimeters, capturing the full diameter where there is no bacterial growth.

- If zones overlap, the experimental design is deemed inadequate; therefore, these measurements should not be reported as they can lead to interpretation errors.

In studies involving extracts or biomaterials (such as dental materials), the literature suggests that wells or discs should be placed at least 24 mm apart (center to center) to avoid overlap (Bauer et al., 1966; Balouiri et al., 2016, Journal of Pharmaceutical Analysis). While the presence of inhibition can be qualitatively reported ("+" or "inhibition present"), it should be noted that overlapping zones hinder quantitative measurement.

Hence, the ROL should look into this including the methodology followed to find its prostic value, which will add further knowledge to the existing body of knowledge. The outcome variables of the study should be well defined before conducting the research. This will help in the designing the study and calculation of an appropriate sample size. The sample size should be calculated using AUC in ROC analysis from published literature.

The outcome measures defined by the study's objectives will determine the role of appropriate statistical methods. The authors have not been able to spell out the outcome measures properly. Hence, the specificity of the use of statistical methods seems vague. This can lead to confusion at a later stage after data collection. Dummy tables and dummy analysis before the execution of the study will be useful.

The Review of Literature (ROL) lacks a finding of NLR as an inflammatory marker. There is literature available on NLR as a prognostic marker in cancer.

The authors have proposed data collection at a single time point, which will have a bias in the analysis as factors like time-to-intervention, dose-response, quality of care, etc., can not be accounted for in the analysis.
